articleTitle: Extended Abstract: Bridging the Academy and the Workplace: Industry Practitioner Perceptions of Engineering Communication Skills
abstract: This project reports on two surveys of industry practitioners regarding engineering communication. Participants were connected to the engineering program on our campus: advisory board members (survey 1) and engineering capstone mentors (survey 2). The surveys focused on the communication demands and priorities of the engineering workplace, with particular attention to the communication work of junior engineers; capstone mentors also provided their perceptions of the communication abilities of engineering capstone students. The survey data extend our understanding of industry communication needs and highlight curricular areas that may need more attention.

articleTitle: Hoodies in the Halls of Power: a Rhetorical Materialist Critique of Professional Decorum in the United States Senate
abstract: This brief paper explores the controversy surrounding Senator John Fetterman’s sartorial choices of casual attire in the hyper-professionalized space of the United States Senate. Fetterman’s clothing choices transcend mere fashion; they embody a statement of class identity and challenge the established power dynamics within the Senate. His attire reflects Pittsburgh’s industrial and labor-oriented history, in contrast to the conventional, affluent image most associated with politicians. Although controversial, Fetterman’s white male privilege minimized the consequences of his indecorous behavior. The reactions to Fetterman’s attire highlight the debate over what constitutes appropriate professional decorum, unveiling the underlying biases and demonstrating how something as mundane as clothing can become a potent symbol in professional and political communication. Through a rhetorical materialist critique of the Fetterman attire controversy, we reveal decorum as a raced, gendered, and imperialistic technology an elite ruling class leverages to preserve the existing order. Our analysis further articulates the implications of Fetterman’s attire regarding material inclusivity and tangible representation in professional settings. We propose that reevaluating traditional decorum standards is essential to accommodate the evolving diversity of modern society.

articleTitle: Carrying Meaning, Bridging Worlds: Indigenous Language Localization in Western Courts
abstract: This work examines the localization practices of Indigenous court interpreters through prototyping and analyzing legal glossaries in eight Indigenous languages from the State of Oaxaca, Mexico. These languages are often needed in Mexican courts and immigration court hearings in the United States. Thus, examining the localization praxes of the court interpreters who use them can provide important intercultural technical and professional communication insights in global contexts. I compare the preliminary results of this ongoing study with the court interpreters' code of ethics from the State of California to demonstrate how Western court assumptions about language interpretation cause gaps between worldviews. This work also shows how court expectations do not always reflect the localization practices of Indigenous court interpreters.

articleTitle: Extended Abstract: The Impact of Interactive AI Feedback on STEM Students' Writing of Lay Research Summaries
abstract: The integration of generative AI tools in academic writing, particularly for STEM students and researchers, is a growing trend. These tools may save time and enhance grammatical accuracy; however, they can also be used pedagogically to help students improve their own academic and science communication skills. Despite this, studies evaluating the impact of AI tools on students' writing outcomes, specifically in STEM, are limited. This research focuses on whether individualized AI-based feedback helps STEM graduate students improve their writing of short research summaries for a lay audience. To this end, students participated in the task in one of four feedback conditions: a group that receives feedback on appropriate jargon use before each iteration; a group that receives interactive feedback from ChatGPT with rewrite suggestions; a group that receives interactive feedback both about jargon and ChatGPT rewrite suggestions; and a comparison group that does not receive any feedback before each rewrite. Results indicate that AI-based feedback helped students improve their use of jargon and readability, though no significant improvement was observed in message distillation. In this presentation, we share the empirical research and available online task for use in STEM academic and science writing programs.

articleTitle: Bridging the Gap: Exploring Barriers and Opportunities of Collaboration in User Experience Partnerships between Nonprofits and (Technical and Professional Communication) Academics
abstract: User experience (UX) is of interest to nonprofits and academics, as these groups may partner to increase students’ UX skill sets while serving local community needs (Lauer & Brumberger, 2016). Focus groups explored perceived barriers and opportunities for UX collaborations between these participants. Findings reveal overlaps in nonprofit and academic values of social justice focused UX, urging them to seek partnerships that are mutually beneficial. Further, findings suggest that Technical and Professional Communication (TPC) faculty are uniquely positioned to assist nonprofits with their UX needs.

articleTitle: Trends in Post-pandemic Instructional Design: An Exploratory Analysis of Job Ads Using Textual Analysis
abstract: With a projected 6% job growth in instructional design over the next decade, the field is thriving. Keeping abreast of trends in the jobs market provides valuable insight to both technical and professional communication (TPC) instructors and practitioners. Although there are some studies reporting on the impact the Covid pandemic had on changing the nature of work for instructional designers, there is a gap in research examining instructional design job ads in the post-pandemic market. As part of an ongoing research project examining over 10,000 instructional design job ads in the U.S. collected between January 2022 and June 2023, this paper uses textual analysis to identify patterns and trends relating to instructional design skills and tools in the post-pandemic jobs market.

articleTitle: A Symbiotic Relationship: Combining User Experience Methods and Systems Theory to Understand Engineering Doctoral Students’ Professional Identity Development
abstract: Studies about doctoral students' professional identity development as scholars and researchers remain scarce within engineering education literature, and current frameworks for tracing identity development require a more effective longitudinal design to capture development over time. As we apply user experience (UX) methods to document students' identity development, we reflect on the affordances and constraints of qualitative user experience methods as a complementary approach to engineering identity research and demonstrate a way of building bridges across disciplines to innovate research methods and scholarly agendas that benefit all partners.

articleTitle: Extended Abstract: Training Engineering Faculty on How to Mentor Scientific Communication: Soft Piloting an Evidence-based Intervention at Rice University
abstract: Graduate students’ ability to confidently communicate scientific information is a critical skill leading to many important student career outcomes, including an intention to pursue or remain in a research career. Faculty advisors play a pivotal role in developing scientific communication (SC) skills, yet rarely receive direct instruction or support in mentoring SC. This abstract presents the pilot of an SC mentoring intervention (SCOARE mentor training workshop) targeting Rice University’s School of Engineering faculty. The next steps include work towards integrating the SCOARE workshop into faculty development programming.

articleTitle: Extended Abstract: East Palestine: Temporal Considerations of Risk Communication
abstract: In response to the Norfolk Southern train derailment in East Palestine, Ohio, on February 3, 2023, and ensuing chemical spill and fire that has impacted air and water of nearby communities, we interview community members about concerns about disaster risk communication. We apply John Dryzek’s ideologies via discourse analysis of participant’s responses. Our preliminary results reveal that residents have considerable short- and long-term environmental and human health concerns about intersecting environmental risk factors that offer insights into complex environmental risk communication models.

articleTitle: Workshop: Building Bridges toward Publication in the Transactions
abstract: This workshop, led by the IEEE Transactions editorial team, offers personalized guidance for manuscript development and publication in IEEE Transactions on Professional Communication. Attendees choose from four tables, focusing on turning conference papers into manuscripts, idea development, revision guidance, or general information. Facilitators, including Editor-in-Chief George Hayhoe, provide targeted feedback and insight.

articleTitle: Workshop: The Challenge of Teaching ‘Effective Written Communication’: Bridging the Gap between Common and Best Practices
abstract: Our workshop addresses the challenge of helping students learn how to communicate effectively in writing. It draws on a scoping review of writing instruction in STEM capstone courses to identify common goals and practices and engages participants in approaches with potential to build transferable capabilities that help students bridge the transition to writing in professional environments.

articleTitle: Extended Abstract: Leveraging AI to Bridge the Gap Between Aspiring Engineers and Effective Communicators
abstract: This extended abstract proposes using the capabilities of open-source large language models (LLMs) to assess rhetorical moves in the executive summaries delivered by students enrolled in a Mechanical Engineering Capstone Senior Design course at a North American public STEM university. Our brief discussion surrounds the national and institutional contextualization of a capstone course, the current state of affairs and drawbacks of the executive summary assessment method, using an LLM to overcome these drawbacks, its potential benefits, and future work.

articleTitle: Bridging the Gap between Executive and Technical Communications
abstract: This paper presents a case study where the existing organizational style guide is insufficient for the specific needs of engineering-based subset of the organization. While the organizational style guide is focused on high-level administrative documents (for instance memos and external communications), it does not provide necessary guidance for technical and engineering-based content. For this case study, a style guide was created by a contractor for use with contractor-developed materials for client delivery. In addition to the style guide, further organizational tools and structures to promote effective technical communication and close the gap with executive communications are presented.

articleTitle: Extended Abstract: Communicate with Ethical Values - Lessons from the Ancient Sangam Literature of Tamil!
abstract: The Sangam period (300 BCE - 300 CE) in Southern India witnessed the emergence of classical Tamil literature, imbued with enduring ethical values. "Aram", epitomizing righteousness, and integrity, permeated the communication of Sangam Kings like Karikalan, offering timeless lessons for today’s discourse. "Inbam", representing love in its various forms, emphasizes empathy and emotional resonance, while "Kodai" underscores compassion and generosity, vital for impactful communication campaigns. "Veeram", the courage to stand up for what’s right in a critical situation. These ancient values, embracing truthfulness, courage, and kindness, remain relevant for crafting messages that inform, inspire, and connect across time. Integrating these principles fosters inclusive communication, reflecting universal brotherhood and humanity.

articleTitle: The Rhetorical Structure of the Entrepreneurial Pitch Problem Statement: Findings from an International Business Accelerator
abstract: This brief paper describes the persuasive strategies used by entrepreneurs for articulating problem statements in their business pitches. Using data from a top international business accelerator, Start Up Chile, we analyzed 44 written problem statements that scored highly on a metric of problem identification. Our findings indicate that when successful entrepreneurs articulate problems/opportunities they employ a cause-and-effect argumentative structure. Their "problem" is described as the result of a societal change or a shortcoming in current products or services, and the effects are pain points experienced in the form of time, money or other resources lost. We also found that the problem statements often explicitly indexed the industry context of the opportunity, used secondary sources to establish ethos, and used rhetorical amplification to create a sense of urgency. We conclude with a template for articulating problem statements. This template may be useful to new entrepreneurs as well as technical and professional communication educators and students.

articleTitle: Bridging People and Practice: Using Design Systems to Teach Accessibility
abstract: Design systems provide a cohesive approach for designers to build, implement, and test products within a unified ecosystem that embeds accessibility throughout the design process. As such, design systems offer a unique approach to help professional/technical communication instructors teach accessibility to their students. This brief paper presents a teaching unit on using design systems to introduce accessibility to students through working with a design system, creating infographics, and revising those graphics through accessibility testing.

articleTitle: Extended Abstract: What We Can Learn From Shifts in Emphasis in Technical Translations
abstract: This research project is the continuation of a study that focused on the translation of technical instructions. The field of technical communication would benefit from more studies on technical translation and a reassessment of the role of translators as primary users of technical documentation. My early study shows that translators will frequently reject word-by-word translation to embrace functional equivalence even when this change of strategies is not strictly necessary or warranted. A future study should focus, more specifically, on how translators manipulate the level of emphasis used in target texts to make them more attuned to different cultural and rhetorical traditions. In general, the idea that translators ‘do’ culture when working on technical documents deserves further investigation.

articleTitle: Design, Training, and Branching Scenarios: Building Bridges through Different User Experiences
abstract: Branching Scenarios are used as instructional strategies in professional and educational training, although it does have challenges when trying to move the approach to professional communication training. This paper introduces the concept of branching scenarios, identifies and acknowledges challenges this approach has when moved to professional communication, and offers ideas that professional communications instructors could use to add branching scenarios strategies into their courses.

articleTitle: Extended Abstract: Designing Research Posters: Empirical Evidence Supports Moving away from Abstracts and Short Section Headings
abstract: Although many online guides claim to provide best practices for designing research (or scientific) posters, little research exists to support these practices. In three small studies we examine readers’ impressions of different poster formats. Our results suggest that most readers prefer posters that use complete sentence headings over those that use headings consisting of a single word or phrase. We also found that readers were divided over the #BetterPosters format, which foregrounds a one-sentence summary of the study and a QR code linking to the full paper, with some readers enthusiastic about this format and others decidedly against it.

articleTitle: Extended Abstract: Delightful Documentation? Improving Documentation Quality with the Kano Model
abstract: A focused, clearly defined, and reader-derived definition of documentation quality is a critical component in collecting meaningful and actionable feedback, creating reliable documentation metrics, and teaching technical communication students how to write quality documentation. To determine how readers define high-quality documentation, I carried out two studies using a set of empirically tested information quality dimensions. In the first study, I found that readers define high-quality documentation as being accurate, relevant, easy to understand, and accessible. In the second study, I used the Kano Model of customer satisfaction to determine how robust this proposed definition of documentation quality was. The results indicated that readers do define high-quality documentation as being accurate, easy to understand, and accessible; however, in this study, documentation completeness replaced documentation relevance. The results of these two studies can provide a sound theoretical basis for focusing on certain dimensions of documentation quality to increase reader satisfaction when writing and teaching. Further research should be done to expand the use of the Kano Model in the field of documentation quality.

articleTitle: Bridging Transformative Possibilities in Engineering Communication
abstract: The objective of this panel is to build bridges across engineering and other technical fields by collaborating on critical pedagogical approaches aimed at meeting the present and future communication challenges facing our students as learners and practitioners. This panel brings together engineering faculty and practitioners based in the US and Canada, representing a range of interdisciplinary backgrounds and career stages, with specializations in technical and professional communication, rhetoric, and civil and environmental engineering. Panelists will share recent pedagogical interventions aimed at preparing engineering students to be reflective technical communicators and transformative members of their profession.

articleTitle: Extended Abstract: Competencies and Connections: Toward Bridging the Academic-Industry Gap
abstract: Bridging the gap between practitioners and academics of technical communication is crucial for ensuring that students are well-prepared for their careers as well as for advancing the field. Literature suggests some strategies that can help address this challenge. In this talk, Ranade and Swarts will discuss case studies from their respective institutions on how they used a combination of strategies to build bridges between their departments and industries in an attempt to close the gap. The case studies will provide practical insights and highlight challenges of implementing the strategies mentioned above along with opening discussions on how to tackle such challenges.

articleTitle: Extended Abstract: Blowing the Whistle: How Nigerians Express Organizational Dissent on Social Media
abstract: This paper explores the rhetorical strategies Nigerians use when they express organizational dissent on social media.

articleTitle: Workshop: Visualising Engineering Communication – Using Systems Design to Understand Communication in an Engineering Project
abstract: In this workshop, participants will be introduced to collaborative systems thinking methodologies designed to map out the lifecycle of engineering projects, capturing the interactions between various stakeholders and processes. Participants will engage in a hands-on visualization exercise. This activity encourages participants to apply visual systems design techniques to projects they are familiar with, allowing them to map out the communication activities from the project’s inception to its conclusion. The intention is to provide a tangible experience of breaking down and understanding the communication interactions in their projects, capturing the ‘who, what, why and how' of these. This exercise is about fostering a deeper understanding and critical thinking about the communication networks at play.

articleTitle: Connecting Accessibility and Engineering/Computing in the Technical Communication Classroom
abstract: In the required Writing in the Disciplines course for undergraduate engineering and computer science students, the authors have developed a project about accessibility that requires students to identify a virtual or physical space (primarily on campus or in the local Buffalo community) and write reports that analyze the accessibility of the site and provide recommendations for improvement. By bridging concepts from Disability Studies and engineering design, the authors aim to help students understand how structural inequities are built into spaces, products, and the digital world. This project also offers students an opportunity to publish their work via the university’s institutional repository. A student survey given after the project’s conclusion demonstrated that students felt they knew more about accessibility and its role in engineering work; however, there was a lack of interest in publishing. This paper describes the project, discusses successes and challenges, outlines plans for moving forward, and offers recommendations for others interested in implementing a similar project.

articleTitle: Current Ethical Stances in Plain Language Research Across Fields
abstract: Currently plain language is studied and used across numerous disciplines and toward many ends. In this pilot study, we built a corpus and coding scheme to track the range of ethical stances taken up by authors studying plain language across various fields, including TPC, health literacy, business and industry, law, the sciences, and others. Overall, our findings show the dramatic dominance of the utilitarian ethical stance across all research, followed by a dialogic ethical stance and others in comparatively few numbers. TPC offers a wide range of ethical stances, including an ethic of social justice unique from the rest of the corpus. This research can help TPC scholars and professionals who operate across these fields to better understand and navigate various ethical priorities. As a pilot, it also serves to begin mapping the terrain for areas of interest for future work.

articleTitle: Building Reflection and Communication Bridges for Broadening of Knowledge in Learned Ignorami
abstract: Reflective writing, as a reflection and communication tool, may help engineers frame their experiences with technical and professional challenges, thus possibly broadening their mindset. We conjecture that it is possible to gauge the broadening of mindset quantitatively. To this end, we have deployed a before- and after- style reflective writing activity in a graduate seminar course. The reflection prompts were developed based on the Entrepreneurial Mindset framework. This framework is a curious, connected, and value-creating way of thinking which fosters problem-solving, critical thinking, etc. These are important dimensions to prepare engineers for the future. We apply hypothesis testing to conduct a quantitative metadiscourse marker analysis of students’ reflections before and after weekly seminars to measure change in students’ mindset. Our analysis framework is applicable to assessing broadening of mindset ranging from individual students in a given semester to separate groups of students over multiple semesters for a longitudinal study.

articleTitle: Teaching Collaborative Problem-Solving in Technical and Professional Communication
abstract: Collaboration is consistently cited as a core competency in workplace communication practices. Previous approaches to teaching collaboration focus on meeting and producing a particular deliverable, or product. Pedagogical approaches to collaborative projects are often based on the media students produce through collaboration rather than assessing collaboration specifically. The authors detail an approach to teaching and assessing collaboration using the Procedural Model for Problem Solving (PMOPS) approach to problem solving in an asynchronous learning environment. Students engage in a problem-solving activity with corresponding assignments that guide students through reflection and critique of collaborative processes, and project assessment focuses on collaborative learning outcomes.

articleTitle: Extended Abstract: Bridging Deep Tech Ethics, Community Literacy, and Computer Science Education
abstract: We present an assignment that leads students through a process of self-reflection, ethical analysis, and collaborative inquiry in a master’s level computer science course that blends professional communication and computing ethics. Students write a case-study narrative involving an ethical "failure" related to their own experiences as computer scientists. Rather than seeking a "right answer," the assignment provides students with an inquiry-based model of ethical decision-making drawn not from abstract principles but from practical wisdom informed by broader social, political, and historical conditions. Because we piloted both the course and the assignment in the spring of 2024, we discuss preliminary insights on the assignment and, more generally, on the possibilities of combining community literacy and deep tech ethics in the computer science classroom.

articleTitle: Visualizing the Entrepreneur’s Journey: Synchronic, Iterative, and Linear Representations
abstract: In this paper, we draw from entrepreneurship literature to develop a typology of visual genres representing "journey"-related aspects of entrepreneurship. We identify and characterize iterative, linear, and synchronic representations of the entrepreneur's journey, providing examples of each from the entrepreneurship literature, and we discuss how these visual genres collectively help neophyte entrepreneurs understand different aspects of their entrepreneurial journey. Finally, we draw implications for entrepreneurship communication and for professional communication more generally.

articleTitle: Workshop: Design fiction as a Novel Approach in Cultivating Critical Reflection and Ethical Awareness in TPC
abstract: This workshop proposal aims to bridge industry practices with teaching methods and merge the fields of design research with professional communication. It focuses on design fiction, a genre that originated from human-computer interaction and interaction design. Design fiction uses "diegetic prototypes" to envision potential changes and critically examines technological impacts, fostering debates over future ethical, social, and political implications without glorifying them. The workshop targets technical and professional communication educators, trainers, and practitioners, offering them insights into integrating design fiction in educational and corporate environments. Attendees will learn to create and utilize futuristic social scenarios, enhancing their critical thinking, creativity, and communication skills.

articleTitle: Successful Problem-Solving in User Support Forums: A Study Aimed at Identifying Post and Thread Characteristics
abstract: User forums are a popular form of user support. Many companies that provide complex products or services host online forums moderated by their employees. On these forums, users discuss problems they encountered with other users and experts. The most prominent advantages of user forums over other types of user support are that users do not have to search for the information they need and that they can get help on their individual problems. Previous studies have investigated various aspects of user forums, but research on what factors influence the success of problem-solving on user forums is scarce. In this paper, we present results of a content analysis of 50 discussions (threads) on user forums. The findings show that most threads were unsuccessful, which means that no solution was presented or not every participant agreed with the presented solution. The results of the analysis of the characteristics of the threads and the individual posts imply that companies should aim to moderate user support forums to keep the threads from becoming too large and that they should encourage users to critically assess suggestions and provide comprehensive information.

articleTitle: Extended Abstract: You Can Lead a Horse to Water: Students’ Usage Patterns of an Open Educational Resource for Technical Communication
abstract: College students frequently skip buying required textbooks. In response, many educators are assigning Open Educational Resources (OER) rather than traditional publisher-created textbooks. Even so, scant empirical evidence exists about whether students actually use these OER. This project addresses this issue by examining Google Analytics data from a free, online Technical Communication textbook. Results indicate that student use of the OER is increasing.

articleTitle: Bridging Divided Disciplines through Interdisciplinary Teaching Collaborations
abstract: This panel answers the question: how might we bridge technical and humanistic disciplines? Further, how might we use the emergent properties of these combined disciplines to cultivate humanistic impulses in our students? The panelists all teach in an Engineering Design program, where students take two years of studio classes co-taught by engineering, computer science, and English faculty. We share examples from our co-teaching experiences over the last few years that illustrate how we’ve bridged disciplines traditionally viewed as divided.

articleTitle: Building Bridges: Five Nonprofit Grant Writers Reflect on Learning the profession
abstract: This presentation features results of an online focus group conversation among five nonprofit proposal writers (also colloquially known as "grant writers") in the early to mid-stages of their careers, reflecting on the roles that job training, mentorship, professional organizations, and a course in nonprofit proposal writing have had on their career knowledge and success. The study found that historical and cultural knowledge of the community, the organization, and the project being funded seemed to be of equal importance to experiences in training or mentoring. The paper shares the experiences of learning these skills within a university level grant writing course and the participants provide recommendations for new grant professionals.

articleTitle: The Impact of an Entrepreneurially Minded Learning Activity on the Metadiscourse of Students’ Reflections
abstract: This work-in-progress investigates the research question: "can entrepreneurially minded-learning (EML) affect the distribution of metadiscourse in student reflections?" As per the Kern Engineering Entrepreneurial Network (KEEN), Entrepreneurial minded learning is a curious, connected, and value-creating way of problem-solving. The EML is a vital disruption to engineering education to better prepare students for the engineering profession. Metadiscourse markers (MDM) are words or phrases that signal the structure or organization of the text to help forge a relationship with the reader and "offer a framework." They are broadly classified into two classes, viz., Interactive and Interactional MDM, which indicate an analytical mindset and an interpersonal engagement with the reader, respectively. Metadiscourse is invariably used in professional communication settings to frame problems or solutions for the benefit of key stakeholders. The metadiscourse embedded in students’ written reflections submitted by two groups of students enrolled in a sophomore-level engineering course on Mechanics of Materials were compared. One group (academic year 2022) experienced a traditional learning activity, while the other (academic year 2023) experienced an EML-motivated learning activity. Statistical analysis of the metadiscourse markers embedded in students’ written reflections suggests that EML may lead to a statistically significant change in analytical and interpersonal engagement-type authorial stance in reflective essays. Conversely, the reflective essays’ analytical and self-reflective nature may be a quantitative indicator of EML and can be directly measured in students’ discourse.

articleTitle: Examining the Accessibility of Generative AI Website Builder Tools for Blind and Low Vision Users: 21 Best Practices for Designers and Developers
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence tools are capturing the attention of the public and business since the introduction of ChatGPT. While this technology offers many productivity tools, their accessibility to screen reader users is little studied. Most of the technical and professional communication research about these tools focuses on their applied potential. This paper reports the findings of a mixed methods study on the user interfaces of three websites on which GenAI tools reside and the accessibility of their web editors. Studying the accessibility of these firms’ websites and their builder platforms is important because without accessibility features, blind customers cannot access these tools and create websites. This study found that none of the three builder websites, or the web editors for their tools, had WCAG 2.1 level AA accessibility. To improve these tools’ accessibility and usability, these website builders will need to invest resources to develop accessibility knowhow on web development and AI. Involvement of disabled users as co-designers and testers is essential to ensure accessibility in this AI infrastructure. This paper contributes 21 best practices for designing accessible interfaces for generative AI tools.

Author Keywords: best practices for generative AI tool design

articleTitle: Meeting ABET Outcomes through Teaching Students to Analyze the Ethics of an AI System
abstract: To address the challenge of meeting ABET outcomes for ethical judgment, communication, and teamwork, this paper presents an innovative team project that integrates these skills and scaffolds their development. The project requires students to analyze the ethics of an AI system by identifying use cases, developing methods of analysis, evaluating such issues as bias, transparency, and sustainability, and developing policy recommendations for improvements to the system or for use in applications. The major deliverables are a collaboratively written proposal and a final team presentation that presents the research and recommendations. Lessons in ethical reasoning; research, information management, and academic integrity; proposal writing; policy advocacy; collaboration; and presentation augment their self-directed study of both how specific AI systems work, and the ethical and sociocultural implications of employing that technology for specific use cases. Students gain both conceptual and applied knowledge of ethical principles, reasoning through complex issues, reaching consensus through structured processes, and analyzing the effects of technology. In addition, students gain an in-depth understanding of the implications of using LLMs in the research and writing process, which increases their ability to make ethical choices about whether to use the output of these systems.

articleTitle: Motor-Mobility Testing for the Enhancement of Web Application Accessibility
abstract: This article outlines a research initiative aimed at enhancing the accessibility of digital platforms, with a particular focus on critical sectors like telemedicine. Collaborating with the Global Partnership for Telehealth (GPfT), the authors are developing motor-mobility testing methods to improve access to essential information, starting with GPfTs Pathways application. Grounded in the revised Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) and Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.0, the study aims to support ADA compliance and disability justice. The research herein offers both testing methods and a means to enhance the delivery of global telehealth information and services as a result of their use. This article offers a comprehensive approach to motor-mobility accessibility testing of the Pathways app, aiming to bridge the gap between education and advancing web application accessibility, ultimately fostering inclusivity online.

articleTitle: Teaching Communication in Context: Rhetorical Moves in Data Science Reports
abstract: This study involves a data science and machine learning course partnered with an engineering communication course—referred to here as an authentically integrated communication model—and offers insights into such a model for engineering educators. In these partnered courses, student teams apply data science and machine learning tools to conduct data analysis and write two data science reports. Through qualitative coding and corpus analysis methods, rhetorical moves that students make in the data science report genre were identified. Twelve out of 57 total final reports were randomly chosen and coded, then six corpora of excerpts related to two codes and subcodes were created to generate keyword lists. These codes were "results," "discussion," as well as "ineffective" and "effective" subcodes for each main code. The total codes were then compared to one another according to students' enrollment in both courses. Overall, students' reports in the engineering communication class more often contained effective results and effective discussion excerpts. Keywords along with example sentences are provided to demonstrate greater context for the use of language in the data science report genre.

articleTitle: Development of a UX Scale for Technical Communication
abstract: This study addresses the need for a standardized scale to evaluate the user experience (UX) of technical documentation, highlighting the role of high-quality documentation in enhancing user support in the fast-evolving technological landscape. Employing a multi-faceted approach, the authors reviewed existing literature, conducted interviews with users, and performed exploratory experiments. This multi-faceted methodology facilitated the identification of key UX dimensions and textual elements within technical documentation, leading to the development of an initial evaluation scale. The scale underwent a series of reliability and validity tests, including cross-validation with existing UX scales and user testing involving documents of varied quality levels. The findings confirmed the effectiveness of the scale in providing nuanced insights into UX of technical documentation. The study successfully generated a reliable and efficient scale tailored for the UX evaluation of technical documentation. This scale enables documentation teams to assess and improve documentation quality based on user feedback, enhancing the overall product experience and potentially boosting market share. By bridging the existing gap in UX evaluation tools specifically designed for technical documentation, the validated scale contributes to the body of knowledge in technical communication.

articleTitle: Diagnosing Communities with the 5Ds: Applying a Framework for Understanding Barriers to Communication and Collaboration in Three Small Texas Communities
abstract: The 5Ds framework—Distance, Diversity, Dilution, Demand, and Disengagement—has been used to better understand barriers to communication and collaboration in regional entrepreneurial ecosystems, including the multi-community regions of Northwest Arkansas and the Aichi Prefecture of Japan, and the country of Panama. Can this framework also be applied to provide insight and guidance to individual communities? In this paper, we attempt to do so. Examining three small towns in Texas, each facing unique social and economic threats, we use the 5Ds to better understand their underlying challenges and how each translates into systemic communication and collaboration issues obstructing community members from working together to solve community problems. After using the framework to diagnose collaboration barriers for each town, we compare these results with each other and with previous community and regional findings. Finally, we explore implications for scaling this approach, especially in professional communication research into communities and improve intra-community communication and planning activities.

articleTitle: Presenting and Making Relevant: A Semantic Frame Analysis of Teaching Assistant Perceptions of Writing in Statistics
abstract: Statistics and Data Science is increasingly attentive to the role of writing in its disciplinary work, and leading voices in the field argue for its inclusion in conceptions of statistical competence. While research has demonstrated that some STEM faculty link writing to professionalism, and others understand it to be integral to the work of the field, there is little research on teaching assistants (TAs) and their perception of writing. Such research is important, given the responsibilities for writing assessment shouldered by TAs in classes taught at scale. This study takes initial steps to respond to this gap by interviewing TAs for an introductory Statistics course at Carnegie Mellon University about writing in their discipline and their perspectives on student writing assessment. Semantic frame analysis identified two salient themes: writing as presentation and contextualization, the latter of which manages to empower audiences with discretionary judgment. Implications for student writing assessment are discussed, before suggesting avenues for future research.

articleTitle: VizCare: Using UCD Techniques to Impact the Child Welfare System
abstract: VizCare is a web-based visualization tool for making research-based evidence available to child welfare professionals. This paper reports on our use of user-centered design (UCD) research techniques to develop, build, and deploy the VizCare tool. This UCD approach included interacting with professionals from across the United States via a usability test and a deployment validation study. Our approach prioritized understanding and addressing the needs of these child welfare professionals who have an interest in using diverse forms of evidence to make informed decisions in child welfare policy and program development work. A key challenge in developing a useful tool in this domain is navigating what counts as valuable data-based evidence and how to communicate it meaningfully to professionals. Our tool integrates evidence from large, government datasets and qualitative, expressed concerns from people with lived experience. VizCare attempts to integrate these different forms of evidence with a previously developed tool called FosterCommViz in a single web-based system.

articleTitle: "It Was Frustrating to Have to Constantly Redesign": An Exploration of Authenticity in Advanced UX Education
abstract: Industry demands professionals who can not only grasp theory but also tackle authentic problems. While traditional user experience (UX) education provides a foundation, developing deep understanding and skills in advanced students requires learning experiences beyond typical in-class projects. This study explores experiential learning experiences of advanced university students through a complex authentic design challenge in a guided student research project, spanning two university quarters. Using an autoethnographic approach, we reflexively analyzed students’ experiences navigating the design challenge within an academic research context. Instead of teaching the basics of UX design, this learning experience focused on hands-on engagement and guided problem-solving. Students applied their design and research skills to tackle new challenges in designing scientific research kits. Through iterative testing, reflection, and collaboration, they identified design gaps, challenged assumptions, and refined their solutions. The study thus emphasizes the importance of experiential learning experiences that challenge students to apply knowledge in authentic, constrained settings and learn from them. The paper concludes with recommendations to educators for leveraging experiential learning in their courses.

articleTitle: Employers’ Perceptions of Microcredentials on Entry-Level Résumés in Technical and Professional Communication
abstract: Increasingly, higher education institutions are investing in a booming microcredentialing industry. These flexible, self-paced courses often promise to improve learners’ hireability through teaching skills that meet market and employer demands. This paper investigates the perceptions of microcredentials within the context of hiring entry-level workers who recently graduated from undergraduate technical and professional writing academic programs. Our qualitative research study reports on the findings from 4 interviews with hiring managers and recruiters in a U.S. metropolitan area. In the guided interview protocol, participants were asked to reflect on their reactions to two sample résumés that included different qualifying credentials. The findings suggest that while microcredentials are appreciated for demonstrating a candidate's initiative and eagerness for self-improvement, they are not yet seen as equivalent to traditional degrees. Portfolios were highlighted as a valuable tool for candidates to demonstrate the practical application of skills, especially when microcredential rigor is in question.

articleTitle: Value Propositions as Fractional Objects: Searching for Strands of Stabilization in a Startup’s Arguments
abstract: Early-stage technology startups must continuously learn: About potential markets and their problems, about the developing technology and its opportunities and limitations, about business models that could sustain an enterprise built around the technology. And they must continuously argue their value to a rotating set of stakeholders. To provide relative stability amidst constant changes to the argument, startups develop a multifaceted value proposition: a claim that can accommodate its diverse stakeholders' values. In this preliminary study, we apply the Orders of Worth framework to archival data and interviews from a startup developing its offering from 2016-2023. We focus on its value proposition, "Save more than you spend," examining how elaborations on this phrase to different stakeholders invoke different orders of worth, yielding what one founder characterizes as a "multifaceted value proposition." We conclude with implications for understanding the value proposition as fractional: cohering just enough to provide a relatively stable project object for the startup.

articleTitle: Looks matter! A Comparative Analysis of Image Use on Chinese and Western Municipal Websites
abstract: The use of images on municipal websites plays a pivotal role in shaping first impressions of local governments and cities. However, our understanding of image usage on municipal websites and its relationship to culture remains limited. This study presents a comparative analysis of image use on 100 Chinese and 100 Western municipal websites, focusing on quantity, image types, and photo themes. The findings reveal distinct patterns: Chinese municipal websites tend to incorporate a significantly higher number of images, prominently featuring icons, posters/infographics, and QR codes, whereas on Western municipal sites relatively more drawings, logos, and photos are shown. These differences suggest that Western municipal websites adopt a text-centric approach, utilizing images primarily for aesthetic and affective purposes. Conversely, Chinese municipal websites adopt an image-centric approach, leveraging images for informative and navigational purposes. Moreover, in terms of photo themes, Western websites predominantly showcase themes related to families and daily life of residents, while Chinese counterparts emphasize government activities and urban development. These disparities reflect differing approaches to audience understanding: sender-responsible in the West and audience-responsible in China. Understanding these distinctions is vital for tailoring municipal websites to specific cultural groups, enhancing user engagement, and effectively communicating the city or government’s image to diverse audiences.

articleTitle: "Homogenize the Markets": Associations and Substitutions in a Startup’s Sociotechnical Arguments, 2016-2023
abstract: Early-stage technology startups must inductively develop a sociomaterial argument that carries out new combinations to provide value. Thus, the startup must prune the field of possible arguments as it tests different combinations, but it also must preserve different possibilities so that it does not prematurely foreclose possible combinations that might be attractive to different markets. Doing so allows the startup to either pivot in case one combination falls through, or "homogenize the markets" by providing a combination that addresses the concerns of multiple markets. In this preliminary analysis, I draw from Schumpeter’s categories of entrepreneurial combinations and from actor-network theorists’ early-1990s scholarship on technical innovations. Based on this scholarship, I examine the associations and substitutions described by a specific startup ("Sapient Engineering") attempting to develop its Internet-of-Things device ("SapienTap"), trying different combinations and substitutions from 2016-2023. I triangulate interviews of Sapient Engineering’s three founders with documents from its archives, documenting how founders attempted to develop combinations that could work for two different markets. I conclude with implications for understanding how startups innovate by establishing, testing, and pruning such combinations to take advantage of new possibilities.

articleTitle: Bridging the Classroom and Workplace: the High-Impact Practices of a Technical and Professional Communication Studio Course
abstract: This paper discusses the high-impact practices of a communication design and content strategy studio course at a regional comprehensive university. A technical and professional communication studio course asks students to work as professional writers in a way that approximates a real-world workplace. The course in this case study, an advanced elective in an English undergraduate program, connected students with community clients to complete projects that integrated research, writing, and design. This paper describes the structure of the course, the design thinking approach applied to client projects, the students ‘ processes, and lessons learned from end-of-term feedback. I conclude with recommendations for similar studio learning experiences that can help technical and professional communication students envision themselves in the professional sphere, bridging classroom and workplace practice through real-world research, writing, design, and project management.

articleTitle: Beautiful Noise? The Impact of Filled Pauses on the Perception of Speaker Charisma
abstract: Research on filled pauses (FPs) in field data of public speeches suggests that, all else equal, oral FPs ("err") are more harmful than nasal FPs ("um") for a public speaker’s perceived charisma. We further examined this conclusion using experimentally varied stimuli and, moreover, by systematically investigating interactions of FP type with two factors: speaker gender and prestige. Secondly, we expanded the focus to a common type of FPs whose influence on speaker charisma has so far never been tested: clicks, better known as ‘tut’ sounds or "tsk". Based on an award-winning investor pitch, 16 stimuli were created by cross-combining gender, prestige, and FP-type conditions. In a balanced randomization design, the stimuli were rated in terms of charisma attributes and two investment-related questions by a total of 237 listeners. Results corroborated the field-data conclusions for male speakers and showed in addition that clicks were more harmful than both oral and nasal FPs, especially for female speakers. Prestige significantly interacted with FP type and gender, e.g., in that female speakers’ charisma perception benefitted more from a prestigious introduction. We discuss our results with respect to their implications for future research and practical application in rhetorical training.

articleTitle: Approaches, Contexts, and Critiques of UX Pedagogy: An Exploration of Themes from an Integrative Literature Review
abstract: As the field of technical and professional communication (TPC) continues to grow and change, graduates of our programs are pursuing careers in emerging sub-fields. UX is one such sub-field that has become central to the overall TPC discipline. However, very little attention has been paid to pedagogical approaches for teaching UX within TPC, though that is starting to change. To foster more work on UX pedagogy, and as part of an ongoing research project examining UX pedagogy literature over the past 20 years, this paper examines approaches, contexts, and critiques of UX pedagogy. We do so by identifying themes from a larger integrative literature review on UX pedagogy.

articleTitle: Gestures and Feet Can Tell Us how You Speak! On the Relationships between Voice and Body Language in VR Public Speeches
abstract: Effective communication hinges on the speaker's delivery, which comprises two non-verbal channels: vocal performance or speech prosody and body language. The two channels interact in complex ways with words – and with each other. And yet, there remains a significant gap in understanding how prosody is linked to or influenced by body language. Our research addresses this gap, investigating correlations of acoustic-prosodic features with the activity patterns of hands and feet. We conducted a study with 28 participants, tasked with delivering a 1-2 minute oral presentation. Using a VR headset, each participant presented in front of a virtual audience. The results not only confirmed expected correlations but also revealed novel insights: (1) Higher gesture rates correlated with more resonant and powerful voices; (2) increased steps per minute led to more silent pauses in speech and less pronounced acoustic indicators for jaw movements, indicating less clear articulation; (3) involvement of both hands resulted in higher pitch levels; (4) standing mainly on heels led to deeper pitch falls and more variable timbre. We discuss the implications of our results for practical speaking training and, more generally, the multi-channel construction of communicative meaning.

articleTitle: Navigating Work-Life Communication Boundaries on Super Apps
abstract: Using interviews as a research method, this study explores workplace communication practices among users of super apps in China, focusing on how these practices affect the management of work-life communication boundaries. Given the prevalent use of super apps in China, these platforms have embedded in people’s daily lives deeply, subtly altering users' communication habits. Using WeChat as an example, this study discusses that the users’ digital workplace communication decisions are often made based on their intuitive understanding of rhetorical situation. This research confirms previous findings that WeChat reinforces the workplace power hierarchy and exacerbates the work-life conflict through the in-depth interviews. Additionally, this paper details tactics employed by users to navigate the blurred boundaries between work and personal life introduced by super apps. These tactics include maintaining separate WeChat accounts for personal and professional use, intentionally delaying responses, muting work-related messages after hours, and carefully managing their social postings. The findings underscore the complex dynamics at play in digital communication environments and suggest avenues for further research into managing digital communication boundaries.

articleTitle: Collaborative Writing for Engineering Learners in India: From a Dormant to a Dynamic Skill
abstract: The Introduction: Engineering undergraduates seem to possess inadequate writing skills, interpersonal skills, and team skills. Though writing is perceived as an individual activity, it is often accomplished in groups at the workplace later. This investigation mirrors the team writing process required at the workplace with the intention of transferring that experience into the engineering classroom. Therefore, this study examines the challenges and benefits of collaborative writing and the strategies to be implemented to develop students’ writing skills in the ESL (English as a Second Language) classroom. Background: In this study, the teacher-researcher gave 14 collaborative writing tasks to two groups of first-year engineering students; they were expected to collaborate as a team and submit their written assignments using Google Docs. Literature review: The literature relevant to collaborative writing and computer-mediated collaborative writing is reviewed here. Methods: This part includes the participants, tasks given, and data-collection tools which comprise the collaborative texts produced in Google Docs, the students’ self-reflective writing, and the interviews with students. Results and discussion: The teacher-researcher analyzed the text produced by each group qualitatively and noticed that students showed a mixed reaction to writing collaboratively. Conclusion: The pedagogical implication is that collaborative writing can promote teamwork and interpersonal communication skills and improve the quality of the work in the ESL classroom.

articleTitle: Bridging Rhetoric and Engineering: Qualitative Results from a Writing Center Program to Improve Engineering Undergraduate Writing
abstract: The lengthy laboratory reports required by upper-division engineering courses typically challenge undergraduates, who may find themselves unprepared to exercise both technical and writing skills together. This paper draws from the results of a multidisciplinary collaboration that trains Writing Center consultants in engineering writing skills. We built on research in "writing transfer" and STEM students, and we engaged in a debate in Writing Center literature over the value of specialist vs. non-specialist consultants. Here, we focus on one intervention in Electrical and Computer Engineering (ECE). Students and consultants received training aligned with classroom teaching for a technical writing assignment. Then, students worked with trained consultants on a draft of their assignment. In addition to completing a quantitative analysis of improvements in student self-efficacy and writing in the intervention, our team collected student responses about the students ’ prior backgrounds in technical writing and their experiences working with the Writing Center consultants. Student comments were used for our qualitative data. This qualitative study discusses the results of our open-coding and concept-driven analyses of written comments by the ECE students. Including student voices in our evaluation offered insights into the students ’ positive experiences bridging academic disciplines with a trained consultant.
